This game has stability problems on MacOS.

This worked for me. The game sometimes crashes without warning after applying this fix for startup:

For people experiencing this issue, Aspyr has responded with a possible fix (it worked for me).
Reinstall Civ VI on Steam
Select 'Play' from your Steam library
After the 'Verifying' prompt appears and completes, close the damaged error prompt, and select cancel.
Then, open your Mac Settings
Select 'Privacy and Security'
Under Security you should see a prompt stating 'Civilization VI was block...'
Click the 'Open anyway' switch under this text
Enter your system password if prompted
Then select 'open' on the prompt
Civilization VI should now launch

What makes it even harder to understand is that games like Dota 2 and Counter-Strike can keep multiple players connected in real time, where every second and every action matters. Civilization VI is a turn-based strategy game. We literally take turns making moves, yet somehow maintaining a stable connection between a few players is still a problem.

Why hasn't this been fixed?

I genuinely love Civilization VI, which is exactly why this is so disappointing. Multiplayer could be fantastic if it were reliable. A game this good and this established deserves a multiplayer system that actually works consistently.

Please fix the multiplayer connection issues. Players shouldn't have to constantly reconnect, reload games, or troubleshoot to finish a game with friends.

The game itself is entertaining, BUT here's my pov: 

I genuinely do not understand why the developers are still restricting multiplayer between Mac and Windows players who aren’t playing together through Steam.

Civilization VI is supposed to be a massive strategy game about building civilizations and competing with other players, yet somehow the developers have managed to make something as basic as playing with friends on different platforms unnecessarily complicated.

If the Mac and Windows versions can communicate and play together through Steam, then why impose these ridiculous limitations on other multiplayer setups? What exactly is the technical or practical reason for preventing players from simply joining the same game?

It’s 2026. Cross-platform multiplayer should not feel like some experimental feature that players have to fight their way through. We shouldn’t have to research obscure compatibility restrictions, find workarounds, or discover after buying the game that we can’t play with our friends simply because we own the game on different platforms.

The game itself is excellent. The multiplayer restrictions are not.

This kind of unnecessary limitation is incredibly frustrating and makes Civilization VI feel much more outdated than it needs to be. And if the developers actually, ACTUALLY care about keeping the multiplayer community alive, then they need to stop putting unnecessary barriers between players on DIFFERENT PLATFORMS.

We all own civ. We paid for it and it really shouldn't be a problem for an old game.

Just let us play.

For thirty years the map was a backdrop with resources scattered on it. Civ VI took the city apart and spread it across the terrain, and suddenly where you put a thing mattered more than what you built.
Districts and adjacency. Builders with charges instead of immortal workers. Policy cards you rearrange between eras. Technologies that arrive cheaper because you went out and did the thing they describe. Every one of those replaced a mechanic that had worked since the nineties, and "it worked" is exactly the excuse that keeps sequels identical for a decade.
And you can't have everything. District slots are gated by population, so every city has to decide what it isn't going to be. The older entries ended with each city owning one of each building; here the good cities are the ones that gave something up.
That takes nerve in a franchise whose audience will happily explain your own game back to you. The people who wrote it off as a mobile game were looking at the colours instead of the tile pressure underneath them.
Not every new balance landed on day one, and it took expansions to settle. It remains the largest structural risk the series ever took, and it came off.
Thirty years of orthodoxy, unstacked. Nobody had to do that, and they did it anyway.

i wish i could give a neutral review, but i guess my opinions are more positive than negative. 

pro: super addictive, CIV VI will eat hours of your day without you even paying attention, it's that easy to get lost in the strategy and puzzles that the game presents. positive feedback loops that make it hard to put down.

pro: each leader gives interesting bonuses, and if you play well, basically any strategy can work.

pro: easy to get into, as the enemy AIs aren't very smart and will usually not get in your way too much on lower difficulties, but super high skill ceiling and potential depth.

pro: CIV VI has a habit of showering the player in rewards that essentially create a positive feedback loop, which is a big reason for the game's addictive nature. specific buildings and wonders will give massive, permanent spikes in productivity, which feels really good.

con: late game can be really slow as you have so many units to move around and cities to manage. the game has a very strong snowball effect where any lead over an opponent can be basically insurmountable, so when you get to that late game you're kinda just going through the motions to reach your victory condition.

con: with a decent PC, most turns are pretty quick, though your mileage may vary. however, in the late game it once again slows down a lot as the game has to calculate so many variables and decisions for the enemy AIs that it can take a full minute for the game to go to the next turn in my experience.

con: you really should get all of the DLC for the best experience, but the game has a comical amount of DLC packs so it's a bit pricy. definitely buy when it's on sale (like right now, when it's only $10).

con: the game is really bad at communicating certain information to the player, and the game is littered with difficult to parse walls of text. i would recommend the "extended policy cards" mod on the workshop at the least, but some issues can't be easily fixed with mods.

This might be the worse-designed game I have ever played, and I've been playing video games since they were invented.

I made a good-faith effort to learn how this game works, but I was met with extreme hostility when I sought out assistance from fans. You have to memorize SO MUCH. Luxuries like Tea span multiple cities, but CERTAIN amenities span 6 tiles, but SOME only affect the current city, and trade routes move "production" (????) from one city to another somehow, and campuses have to go near mountains (why????) and you can't upgrade your units unless you select this SPECIFIC TECH way down at the bottom (despite already having rocketry and satellites) and if you don't upgrade your units, the XP goes to waste and it doesn't TELL you to upgrade your units. The World Congress ungrays the "Next" button if you spend all your points, so the bad design makes you THINK you HAVE to spend all your points when you don't have to. It's possible to purchase policy changes, but if you lack the gold, the button is completely hidden, so it's possible for the game to NEVER tell you about this mechanic. The game doesn't tell you the pros/cons of open borders or explain that zealots IGNORE borders, or that sending an Envoy to a "Technological" state will boost YOUR tech (why?????). It has icons that look like cities, but it turns out those are just "suggestions" and you can actually plop a city anywhere. Same thing with farms, mines, etc., the icons are misleading. The advisor LITERALLY LIES to you to make you lose, so the new-user experience is awful to begin with. You found a religion and gets tons of faith points, but you can't spend them on anything unless you "build" an Apostle (for some reason?) and the game doesn't explain that OR tell you how to GET an apostle. The tutorial shows you the very basics, but only like, "Here's the purchase screen." It doesn't explain WHY you build ANYTHING or any of the win conditions or what sorts of obstacles you should prepare for. But if you need a tutorial to explain how to click buttons, they got you. You can't learn as you play because it doesn't explain why Spain suddenly, randomly got a Diplomatic Victory or why your units can't compete with another city's units despite the fact that you've been playing for the same number of turns and they're the SAME UNIT. It doesn't explain why building a Taj Mahal gives you a benefit. (Trump destroyed the reflecting pool and nothing happened, so I know that stuff doesn't matter IRL.) There are tons of bonuses to be had, like if you build multiple units of a type, it boosts some Tech or Civic, but none of it makes sense! You wind up doing random things to get bonuses and it's soooo unfocused. Like, I built 3 archers I didn't need, NOW WHAT? Do I just delete those now? It's so dumb.

And if you get a bad start, you could be doomed to lose no matter what you do, so all of that above might not even matter.

Nothing is explained anywhere, nothing just "makes sense" intuitively, and you will be insulted if you ask for help.

An enjoyable civilization game. Each one is a little different. I'd recommend reviewing all Civ games and identifying which one suites you best if you can only purchase one. None are "better" or "worse," but take a different path in the gameplay.

This one utilizes a mechanic where you can, over time with technology, combine up to 3 same units, as well as have certain supporting units working together to improve performance.

The gameplay focuses, from my perspective, on military and religion for unit movement. There are other elements, such as building natural parks and utilizing archeologists to pull ancient artifacts from the ground to improve tourism, which is one method of winning.

All in all, this is a great game that you can sink a few hours into or a lot more than that.

Sid Meier’s Civilization VI is one of my favorite games because it gives me an incredible feeling of progression and accomplishment. I love being able to choose a civilization and leader, start with almost nothing, and then watch my nation develop through thousands of years of history. There is something extremely satisfying about seeing a small settlement grow into a massive empire and knowing that the decisions I made along the way shaped its development.

One of my favorite mechanics is the progression through the different Ages. I really enjoy how the game rewards you for performing well during an Age and can also punish you if your civilization falls behind. It makes each era feel meaningful instead of simply being another step toward the end of the game. I especially like the feeling of entering a new Age and seeing how much my civilization has changed, both technologically and culturally.

The gameplay and mechanics are excellent, and there is so much variety in how you can approach each game. Different leaders, civilizations, technologies, governments, districts, diplomacy, religion, culture, and military strategies all give you different ways to build your empire. Every game can feel completely different depending on the civilization I choose and the decisions I make.

I also have to give special praise to the music. The soundtrack is easily one of my favorite parts of the game. I love how the music evolves alongside your civilization, beginning with more tribal and primitive sounds and gradually becoming more complex and grandiose as you progress through the Ages. Hearing the music develop alongside my civilization makes the passage of time feel much more significant and gives the game an incredible atmosphere.

If I had one major criticism, it would be the late game. Once my civilization becomes a massive empire with dozens of cities and countless things to manage, the amount of micromanagement can become tedious. By that point, managing every city, unit, district, and decision can sometimes feel more like work than gameplay. I still enjoy reaching that point, but I wish there were better ways to automate some of the repetitive tasks.

Aside from that, Civilization VI is a 10/10 experience for me.

[h1]Civilization VI is easy to learn, difficult to master.[/h1]

Typically, whichever Civ entry you play first is the one that ends up becoming your favorite. Civ V was mine, and it stayed that way for many years. But nowadays, after numerous updates and expansions, Civ VI has become the entry I enjoy playing the most—especially since it's a game my wife and I love playing together.

You'll start as a leader with a small settlement, build your civilization from the ground up as you explore the world, develop your cities, advance your technology and culture, and interact with the civilizations around you while trying to win the game.

And there's a lot to figure out along the way. Dozens of civilizations and leaders, multiple victory conditions, different maps, governments, religions, districts, wonders, Great People, diplomacy, trade, espionage, city-states, unique units and buildings. Not to mention the enormous technology and civics trees.

What makes Civilization games special, however, is that you don't need to understand all of the mechanics ([i]which are really just scratching the surface of what's there[/i]) to have a great time. You'll play a game, make some poor decisions, learn from them, apply what you've learned in the next game, and then come back with a completely different strategy that may or may not work for you.

[b]But whether you're a beginner or a veteran, the game is just simply fun to jump in and play.[/b]
